blocks.text: Self-consistency prompting extends chain of thought, covered in the previous topic, by generating several independent reasoning paths for the same question and taking the answer most of them agree on, rather than trusting a single reasoning attempt.

This topic covers how self-consistency actually works, why sampling multiple diverse paths and voting improves reliability over a single attempt, the real cost of running multiple model calls, and when that extra cost is genuinely worth paying.
1. What Self-Consistency Prompting Means

blocks.alt: Building on chain of thought, self-consistency prompting samples multiple reasoning paths and votes

blocks.text: Self-consistency runs the same chain of thought prompt multiple times, allowing the model to generate a somewhat different reasoning path each time, then selects the final answer that the largest number of these independent paths actually agree on.
2. Generating Multiple Independent Reasoning Paths

blocks.alt: The same prompt produces reasoning path 1, path 2, and path 3 independently

blocks.text: Rather than asking once and trusting the result, self-consistency asks the same question several times, with some randomness in generation allowing each attempt to reason through the problem slightly differently, arriving at its own independent final answer.

code.content:
answers = []
for _ in range(5):
    response = model.generate(cot_prompt, temperature=0.7)
    answers.append(extract_final_answer(response))

final_answer = most_common(answers)

blocks.text: 3. Majority Voting on the Final Answer

blocks.alt: Path 1 and path 2 agree on answer A, path 3 lands on answer B, the majority vote picks A

blocks.text: Once several independent reasoning paths each produce a final answer, self-consistency simply takes whichever answer the majority of paths agree on, this voting step is what turns several individually imperfect attempts into a single, more reliable final result.

blocks.text: 4. Why Diverse Reasoning Paths Improve Reliability

blocks.alt: A single reasoning path leaves one error uncaught, multiple paths rarely make the identical error

blocks.text: A single chain of thought attempt can go wrong at any individual step, and that error then propagates silently to a wrong final answer, when several independent paths reason through the same problem differently, an error made in one path rarely gets repeated identically across most of the others, making the majority answer more trustworthy.

blocks.title: This mirrors a familiar idea from statistics and ensemble methods
blocks.content: Combining several independent, imperfect estimates into a single vote or average, a pattern that shows up across many areas of machine learning, tends to produce a more reliable result than trusting any single estimate alone.

blocks.text: 5. The Real Cost, Multiple Model Calls

blocks.alt: One model call is compared against several independent model calls

blocks.text: Self-consistency multiplies both cost and latency directly by the number of independent paths sampled, five reasoning attempts cost roughly five times what a single chain of thought call would, covered in the earlier discussion of token cost in the Tokens and Tokenization topic, this cost has to be weighed against the reliability gain.
6. When Self-Consistency Is Worth the Extra Cost

blocks.alt: A high stakes answer justifies self-consistency, a low stakes answer where speed matters more can skip it

blocks.text: Self-consistency earns its cost for genuinely high stakes questions, ones where getting the answer wrong has a real consequence, and where the underlying task benefits from the reasoning diversity, for low stakes, high volume, latency sensitive use cases, a single chain of thought pass is often the more practical choice.
7. Controlling Path Diversity Through Sampling Settings

blocks.alt: A sampling temperature setting controls how diverse the reasoning paths turn out to be

blocks.text: The diversity across the independently sampled reasoning paths is controlled by the model sampling temperature, a moderate temperature setting introduces enough variation for the paths to genuinely differ, while too high a setting can make individual paths unreliable on their own, a related concern covered in more depth in the LLM APIs Fundamentals module.
8. Self-Consistency vs a Single CoT Pass

Chain of thought alone, covered in the previous topic, is a single attempt at reasoning through a problem, self-consistency is specifically the addition of running that same attempt multiple times and voting, the two techniques are not competitors, self-consistency is a direct extension built on top of chain of thought.
9. Practical Implementation Considerations

Implementing self-consistency requires an application to make several model calls per user request and aggregate the results programmatically, this adds real implementation complexity beyond a simple single call prompt, worth factoring in alongside the direct cost when deciding whether to use this technique.
Worked Example

A team building a financial calculation assistant runs a single chain of thought call for a complex multi step calculation and occasionally gets a wrong final number due to a single arithmetic slip mid reasoning.

Switching to self-consistency, sampling five independent reasoning attempts and taking the majority answer, the same calculation now reaches the correct final answer consistently, since an occasional individual arithmetic slip rarely repeats identically across all five independent attempts.
Common Mistakes

items: Applying self-consistency to low stakes, high volume requests where the extra cost is not actually justified
Using a sampling temperature so low that all reasoning paths end up nearly identical, defeating the purpose of voting
Not accounting for the multiplied cost and latency when deciding whether to use this technique in production
Assuming a majority vote guarantees a correct answer, when it only improves reliability rather than providing a certainty

blocks.text: Practice

Take a multi step reasoning problem, run a chain of thought prompt against it five separate times with some sampling randomness, record each final answer, and check whether a majority vote across those five attempts matches the actual correct answer more reliably than any single attempt alone.
Key Takeaway

Self-consistency prompting samples several independent chain of thought reasoning paths for the same question and takes the majority answer, improving reliability over a single attempt by reducing the impact of an isolated reasoning error, at the real cost of multiple model calls, making it worth reserving for genuinely high stakes questions.
